articles.title: Green Party deputy leader Mothin Ali linked to property lets in Leeds
articles.summary: Mothin Ali, is linked to two rental properties via his company, but does not appear to profit from them.
articles.body:
The deputy leader of the Green Party, Mothin Ali, is linked to two buy-to-let properties, despite his party's opposition to private landlords.

Ali is the sole director of a company, which he set up and controls, that owns two rental properties in Leeds, bought in June 2022 and March 2025 - although he does not appear to profit from either of them.

The property purchases happened before the Greens adopted a policy committing to phasing out ownership of rental properties by private landlords in October 2025.

The Green Party told the BBC that, at the time Ali had set up the company, and since, he "has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities".

Ali's connection to the rental properties via real estate company MA Holdings, which purchased them with buy-to-let mortgages, was first reported by the Times newspaper.

Records held by Companies House show that Ali is the sole director of MA Holdings, incorporated in December 2021, and he is listed in the records as the sole person with significant control, owning more than 75% of the shares.

The company's business includes "buying and selling of own real estate", "letting and operating of own or leased real estate" and "management of real estate on a fee or contract basis".

The BBC has spoken to the previous owner and resident of the second property, who confirmed that Ali's company had purchased the property and believed it was bought with the intention to be let out.

Asked why MA Holdings owns the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson said: "We have provided deeply personal information to the BBC in confidence which shows that Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities.

"At Councillor Ali's request, we are not going to make this information public to protect his family."

The BBC is not publicising the personal information shared with it, at the request of the Greens, as it relates to private family matters.

In October last year, delegates to the Green Party's annual conference, passed a motion titled "Abolish landlords" , headed "the private rental sector has failed, it is a vehicle for wealth extraction, funnelling money from renters to the landlord class".

The motion states: "The effective abolition of private landlordism and the private rented sector, coupled with the mass expansion of council housing, is the only way to end the housing crisis."

This is now official policy for the Green Party of England and Wales, with a plan to increase regulation and taxes on private rentals to make it difficult for landlords to make a profit, while boosting housebuilding by councils.

The policy would use existing Green policies such as imposing rent controls, ending buy-to-let mortgages and giving councils the right to buy a rental property when it is sold at a discounted price.

Asked whether Ali had sought to take any steps since the policy had been adopted to change anything with regard to the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson told the BBC he fully supported the policy.

"The policy does not literally seek to abolish landlords, but rather to put in more regulations and taxes on private rentals through measures such as rent controls and expanded social housing," they said. "All of which Mothin Ali supports."

When the policy was introduced, Green Party MP Carla Denyer told the BBC "while the motion to conference had an eye-catching name, it does not actually 'abolish' landlords".

"It does, however, address the housing crisis, empowers tenants and improves their wellbeing," she added.

"It contains a range of policies which, over time, would reduce the proportion of the housing market that is privately rented, and increase the proportion of socially rented homes."

articles.title: In 2015, Mark Pentecost paid $14.5 million for a 104-acre Florida island; after pouring millions into upgrades, it is asking $89 million with a 9-hole golf course and 29 developable lots
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Eleven years after buying a private retreat off Florida’s west coast for $14.5 million, entrepreneur Mark Pentecost has listed the 104-acre property f.
articles.body: Eleven years after buying a private retreat off Florida’s west coast for $14.5 million, entrepreneur Mark Pentecost has listed the 104-acre property for $89 million after spending millions on its transformation. The estate, historically known as Little Bokeelia Island, was listed through Coldwell Banker Realty and featured in Realtor.com's round-up of high-value American homes. The sharp rise in its value follows major improvements, including a private nine-hole golf course, upgraded infrastructure and 29 developable residential lots.From classroom teacher to island ownerPentecost, a former high-school mathematics teacher and basketball coach, made his fortune after founding the multi-level marketing company It Works! in 2001. The health and beauty business grew into a company worth hundreds of millions of dollars, allowing Pentecost and his wife, Cindy, to buy the island in July 2015. The couple paid much less than the property's original asking price of $29.5 million. At the time, the sale was recorded as one of the most expensive residential property deals in South-West Florida. Speaking shortly after the purchase, Pentecost described his vision for the private retreat. “Little Bokeelia is a slice of paradise that allows you to enjoy friendship, fun, freedom and to unplug from the chaos of today,” Mark Pentecost said in a statement released at the time. “It's in these moments when you're able to relax that you can brainstorm and innovate.”Historical roots and modern upgradesLocated in Pine Island Sound between Sarasota and Naples, the island has a history dating back to the early 20th century. Industrialist and dry-cell battery inventor Charles Frederick Burgess bought the property in 1924 and built a Spanish-style villa in 1928. He hosted notable guests there, including inventor Thomas Edison. During his 10 years of ownership, Pentecost transformed the island into a fully equipped corporate retreat and family compound. The estate is centred around the restored 1920s Addison Mizner-style main mansion, along with four guest cottages, a clubhouse, a caretaker's home and several recreational facilities. Together, the buildings contain 11 bedrooms, 10 full bathrooms and three half-baths. Along with the new nine-hole golf course, the property now has a pickleball court, full tennis and basketball courts, four deep-water docks, a resort-style swimming pool and a commercial-grade helipad for travel to and from the mainland. Property records from listing brokerages Coldwell Banker Realty and SWFLMLS show that the estate covers 104 acres with a large amount of shoreline. The 29 subdivided, developable lots could allow a future owner to turn the private island into an exclusive residential community or keep it as one large estate.Market positioningWith an asking price of $89 million, Little Bokeelia Island is now among the most expensive private island properties listed in the United States. Property records show annual taxes of about $115,166. Although the island is secluded and can only be reached by helicopter or boat, it is close to deep-water tarpon fishing and coastal areas near the historic Gasparilla Inn on nearby Boca Grande. Coldwell Banker and Pentecost's representatives have not publicly said whether the property will be sold as one unplatted parcel or whether developers will be able to buy individual subdivided lots. The sale is one of the most notable private island property offerings on the Gulf Coast in recent decades.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Why potluck parties are making a big comeback in America
articles.summary: As Americans spend less time socialising, communities are rediscovering an old way of bringing people together.
articles.body:
Trenton, New Jersey — Long tables covered with American-flag tablecloths stand ready in the summer heat, as red, white and blue balloons sway overhead. The few dishes that have arrived are tucked under white mesh covers, while two grills sit at the edge of a driveway across the street.

Small American flags line the path to this grassy area beside a canal and a patch of trees. The trail begins at a large, dark burgundy sign that reads, “Welcome to Hiltonia, founded circa 1920”. The quiet neighbourhood of about 300 single-family homes, well-kept lawns and tree-lined streets is part of Trenton, New Jersey.

Only a handful of residents are mingling as Rich Green and Julie Kroon, a young couple in matching blue T-shirts, arrive with a bowl of corn and bean salad. Soon, others show up, greeting one another enthusiastically as they compliment the festive outfits and ask what everyone has brought to eat. As some struggle to open their folding chairs, others step in to help.

Thomas Emerick, a Hiltonia resident for 26 years, stands near the food table. Wearing a red-and-white striped shirt, he points to his contribution: a Thai black bean salad flavoured with garlic, ginger, cilantro and lime juice.

“You know what? You can have a social event without food, and you know how many people are going to come?” he asked. “Exactly. Now, if you feed them, they will come.”

Hiltonia’s gathering was part of America’s Potluck, a nationwide initiative led by the America250 Utah Commission to mark the country’s 250th anniversary through shared meals. But it also reflected a broader effort to rebuild social ties through one of the oldest social rituals: eating together. As loneliness and social divisions grow in the United States, communities, nonprofits and governments are turning to potlucks, communal dinners and other food-based gatherings to create opportunities for connection. Experts say these meals can bring neighbours to the same table, but lasting relationships depend on what happens after the dishes are cleared.

The July 5 America’s Potluck initiative encouraged people in every state to host or attend a potluck, with communities in all 50 states participating . While organisers had intended it to be a one-off event, they said some hosts are already preparing to do it again next year. Hiltonia was one of more than 1,700 such potlucks that took place across the country.

Dressed in a red sleeveless dress and sunglasses, Lily Knezevich, president of the Hiltonia Association, greeted everyone and made sure things were running smoothly at the event. A Hiltonia resident for more than 20 years, Knezevich learned about America’s Potluck through her involvement with Revolution NJ, New Jersey's initiative for organising semiquincentennial events.

The Hiltonia Association tries to keep people engaged with one another and encourages neighbours to support and look out for each other, Knezevich explained. Food is one way to make this happen.

“People naturally like to get together around food,” she said. “It's a great draw.”

Getting people to a table, of course, is the easy part. The tougher question is whether a meal can turn strangers into neighbours and friends — and whether a few hours of togetherness can build lasting connections. Research cannot yet tell us how long those relationships last, but it is beginning to shed light on the social benefits of eating together.
